To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a tip calibration is essential for a quantitative interpretation of tunneling spectra of single atoms or molecules, and (2) the two methods presented here allow a quantitative interpretation of spectra acquired with different tips.
(a) background subtraction is possible for single atom and molecule spectra and (b) that it allows to extract tip-independent spectra from experimental spectra with an accuracy of 10 meV.

the two background subtraction methods, (i) subtraction of the tip spectrum from the sample spectrum and (ii) subtraction of the spectrum of a clean metal surface from the sample spectrum, both yield reliable background-free spectra.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods to extract the intrinsic properties of single atoms and single molecules on metal surfaces by scanning tunneling spectroscopic means.
the atomic scale spectroscopic characterization of single atoms and molecule on metal surfaces.
the development and application of methods for data treatment in atomic scale tunneling spectroscopy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the two methods are complementary and can be applied for the removal of the spurious tip background signals in tunneling spectroscopy, and thus allow to extract the intrinsic information from the sample.
the method of background removal by subtraction of the tip-induced spectrum of a clean surface is the most reliable and most robust.
background removal is possible and can be achieved with high precision, if the tip is properly characterized on the clean metal substrate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the background removal is a necessary tool in the interpretation of STM spectroscopy and it should be used in all cases in which the tip apex is changed.
we developed a new method to extract the true tip-independent electronic density of states of single atoms on surfaces from low temperature tunnel spectra.
the presented methods allow for the extraction of the true electronic properties of single atoms and single molecules at surfaces from scanning tunneling spectra.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it provides a simple and efficient way to remove tip-induced artifacts in tunneling spectroscopy.

background subtraction can be applied to scanning tunneling spectroscopic data with the aim of removing artifacts introduced by the tip and to reveal the intrinsic spectral properties of the system under investigation.
background removal in tunneling spectroscopy is a well defined procedure that is not limited to the case of a single adsorbate on a clean metal substrate.
